Q: Why doesn’t copy-pasting from a terminal preserve the original bytes? A:

Always use file input and output for data that could be binary. It doesn't have to be actual files, just file like. For example, reading from standard input and writing to standard output works fine.

With that said, if the data is not textual, then use pipes or redirection to read and write data.

For example, to read text data and write to a file you can do something like this ($ is the prompt and ^D is control-D (on Windows use Control-Z instead)):

$ ./my_encoder > my_binary_file
Some text that should be encoded in some binary format.
^D
$

If the program writes to standard output, a file named my_binary_file will be created and hold whatever you write to standard output (text or binary).

Then to do the opposite:

$ ./my_decoder < my_binary_file
Some text that should be encoded in some binary format.
$

When the my_decoder program reads from standard input, it will read the data from my_binary_file. What it writes on standard output will be written to the terminal.

This also works with pipes:

$ cat my_binary_file | ./my_decoder
Some text that should be encoded in some binary format.
$

[NB: cat is a Linux and macOS command that can be used to type or output the contents of a file. On Windows type can be used this way.]

Or even for both encoding and decoding:

$ echo "Some text that should be encoded in some binary format." > my_text_file
$ cat my_text_file | ./my_encoder | ./my_decoder
Some text that should be encoded in some binary format.
$

Or perhaps a combination of redirection and pipes:

$ echo "Some text that should be encoded in some binary format." > text_input_file
$ ./my_encode < text_intput_file | ./my_decode > text_output_file
$ cat text_output_file
Some text that should be encoded in some binary format.
$

What you can't do, as explained by Remy Lebeau, is to paste arbitrary binary data into the terminal.

Q: Plymouth BGRT theme with console logs A:

the script module doesn't natively inherit the BGRT framebuffer like the dedicated C plugin does. Most folks just bundle the vendor logo as a PNG in a script theme to "fake" the BGRT look. For the logs, are you trying to show the full dmesg stream or just the systemd status messages?

Q: Restir implementation exibits strong ghosting A:

It is because visibility on reused temporal samples is never re-tested

Pass order in RestirApp.cpp:226-235:

GBuffer → RIS → Visibility → Temporal → Spatial → Shading

VisibilityPass traces a shadow ray for the current-frame reservoir against the current BVH, then never runs again. Inside combineReservoirs, the previous-frame reservoir r2 carries a light sample whose occlusion was evaluated against the previous frame's BVH from the previous shading point. combineReservoirs re-evaluates BRDF and NdotL at the new P/N but does not re-test visibility.

Forward camera motion produces disocclusions: surfaces newly exposed because foreground has moved aside. The reused sample was unoccluded from the previous foreground surface but is occluded from the newly visible background surface. With min(5 * M_curr, M_prev), the stale sample persists 5–20 frames, producing the observed smear. Backward motion produces occlusions rather than disocclusions. Reprojection from a current background pixel lands on the same surface in the previous frame, so reservoirs are consistent and no artifact appears.

To fix, trace a shadow ray from the current shading point to the previous reservoir's light sample before combining (ReSTIR DI, unbiased variant):

float  Ll = length(L);
RayDesc ray = { currP, 0.001, L / Ll, Ll };
ShadowRayData sd; sd.hit = true;
TraceRay(gScene.rtAccel, RAY_FLAG_ACCEPT_FIRST_HIT_AND_END_SEARCH,
         0xFF, 1, rayTypeCount, 1, ray, sd);
if (sd.hit) previousReservoir.m_W = 0.0f;

also

const float prevlinearDepth = gPreviousNormalWs[pixel].w;               // incorrect
const float prevlinearDepth = gPreviousNormalWs[previousPixelPos].w;    // correct
